title: Relative Clauses with the Subjunctive, Participle Overview

blocks.text: 56.1 Relative Clauses of Characteristic
In chapter 25 we saw relative clauses that use the relative pronoun (quī, quae, quod) and an indicative verb, such as these examples.
vir quem vidēs rēx est. ‘The man whom you see is the king.’
librum quem legis scrīpsī. ‘I wrote the book that you are reading.’

Sometimes, however, relative clauses have verbs in the subjunctive (the tense is determined by normal sequence of tenses: see chapter 46.2, not chapter 54). These subjunctives can have a variety of meanings, which must be distinguished primarily by context. The most important of these meanings is a generalizing function known as the ‘relative clause of characteristic’; this is used to indicate that the subject has the characteristics that would cause the action of the verb, rather than that the subject necessarily does cause the action of the verb. is nōn est quī illud faciat. ‘He is not a person who would do that.’ / ‘He is not the sort of person who does that.’
nēmō est quī hoc crēdat. ‘There is no-one who would believe this.’

sunt quī hoc crēdant. ‘There are those who would believe this.’ ille liber est quem omnēs Rōmānī legant. ‘That is a book that all the Romans would read.’ / ‘That is the sort of book that all the Romans read.’ versus ille liber est quem omnēs Rōmānī legunt. ‘That is the book that all the Romans are reading.’
Translate:
nemo est qui istum laudet.
sunt qui pugnare nolint.
is est qui omnia audeat.
hi sunt versus quos omnes legant.
erant qui dicerent alios non advenisse.
nihil erat quod facere possemus.
quis est qui hoc credat?
libros scripsit quos nemo legeret.
sunt qui inimicis ignoverint.
nemo erat qui bene pugnaret.
Translate into Latin using relative clauses with subjunctive verbs:
There is nothing that others can do now.
There were those who would give the queen gifts.
He is the sort of man who frees his slaves.
There was no-one who would have wanted to go.
There are those who would always fear other men.
He said the sort of words that persuade everyone.
He is not the sort of person who carries off other men’s money.
He was the sort of person who helps others.
56.2 Relative Clauses of Purpose and Cause
Sometimes a relative clause with subjunctive verb is equivalent to a purpose clause; this occurs only with certain types of main verb, including ones meaning ‘send’, ‘go’, and ‘come’.
mīlitēs mīsit quī oppidum dēfenderent. ‘He sent soldiers to defend the town.’
trēs virī vēnērunt quī rēgī persuādērent. ‘Three men came to persuade the king.’

Alternatively, a relative clause with subjunctive can express cause; under these circumstances the particle quippe is often placed in front of the relative pronoun. mīlitēs quippe quī fūgissent interfectī sunt. ‘The soldiers were killed because they had fled.’ hanc puellam quippe quae pulcherrima sit maximē amō. ‘I greatly love this girl because she is very beautiful.’
Translate: 374 Relative Clauses with the Subjunctive, Participles
Athenas iverunt alii qui nostros captos invenirent et liberarent.
iuvandus mihi est ille quippe qui vitam meam servaverit.
nemo erat qui nihil regi afferret.
Syracusas misit duos milites qui pecuniam amissam invenirent.
alter, quippe qui nesciret, rogavit unde missi essemus.
is non est qui uni amico donum magnum det et aliis nihil.
Londinium venerunt multi qui reginam novam viderent.
alii, quippe qui servi sint, haec domum ferent.
sunt qui dicant te servos tuos liberavisse.
servum Romam mittam qui epistulam tuam mihi afferat.
Translate into Latin using relative clauses with subjunctive verbs:
We sent slaves to the river to drive the sheep out of the water.
My father, because he knew these things, spoke with the king.
There is nothing that that man does not know.
Soldiers of the king came to lead us to Corinth.
Our mother, because she is at home, will persuade our father to forgive us.
He is the sort of man who fears nothing.
Other men will go to Carthage to persuade the queen.
56.3 Participles: Summary of Formation
Before embarking on the next chapter it will be useful to look again at participles, which we saw in chapters 6.2, 21.3, 24, and 32. The available participle forms are:

56.4 Reading Practice

1 Livy, Ab urbe condita 1.9.1–2: the historian explains the problems that led the early Romans to steal the Sabine women (written in the first century bc about a much earlier and partly mythical period).

Iam res Romana adeo erat valida, ut cuilibet finitimarum civitatum bello par esset; sed penuria mulierum hominis aetatem duratura magnitudo erat, quippe quibus nec domi spes prolis nec cum finitimis conubia essent. tum ex consilio patrum Romulus legatos circa vicinas gentes misit, qui societatem conubiumque novo populo peterent.
Vocabulary

rows: quīlibet, quaelibet, quidlibet (declines like quī) ‘any one’
Relative Clauses with the Subjunctive, Participles
2 Martial 2.20: another way to become a poet (first century ad).

blocks.text: Carmina Paulus emit. recitat sua carmina Paulus.
nam quod emas possis iure vocare tuum.
Vocabulary
3 Cicero, Epistulae ad Atticum 10.3 (adapted): Cicero asks his friend Atticus anxious questions about the war between Caesar and Pompey in 49 bc .

Cicero Attico salutem dicit. cum quod scriberem plane nihil haberem, haec autem reliqua essent quae scire cuperem: num Caesar profectus esset, quo in statu urbem reliquisset, in ipsa Italia quem cuique regioni aut negotio praefecisset, ecqui essent ad Pompeium et ad consules ex senatus consulto de pace legati – cum igitur haec scire cuperem dedita opera has ad te litteras misi. feceris igitur commode mihique gratum si me de his rebus et si quid erit aliud quod scire opus sit feceris certiorem. ego in Arcano opperior dum ista cognosco.
Vocabulary

rows: opus est (+ infinitive) ‘it is necessary to’
praeficiō, praeficere, praefēcī, praefectum (+ X accusative and Y dative) ‘put X in charge of Y’
ecquī ‘whether any’ (agrees with lēgātī) cōnsul, cōnsulis (m.) ‘consul’

blocks.text: 4 Martial 11.50: the reputation of Virgil in the later first century ad. Silius Italicus was an important composer of imperial-period Latin epic.
Iam prope desertos cineres et sancta Maronis nomina qui coleret pauper et unus erat.
Silius orbatae succurrere censuit umbrae, et vatem vates non minor ipse colit.
Vocabulary

rows: pauper et ūnus erat ‘there was only one man, a pauper’
succurrō (like currō) (+ dative) ‘come to the help of’
Marō, Marōnis (m.) was the cognomen of P. Vergilius Maro, now known as ‘Virgil’
